newsitem.title: UK: AMB - German brewery launches kosher beer.
newsitem.headline: AMB - German brewery launches kosher beer.

text.p: Rabbi Alan Plancey drains his glass appreciatively. "I am very taken with this," he says, tasting the first kosher beer launched in Europe.

Herrenhauser, a medium-sized brewery in Hanover, Germany, hopes to exploit a lucrative niche market with the beer, made to strict kosher standards. "At the beginning, to be honest, I thought it was a gimmick. But people want to know what they are buying," Plancey said.
The beer, like any German pilsner, is made using only water, malt, hops and yeast.
But Willy Ungar, chairman of the Kashrut or kosher foods committee of the Federation of Synagogues in London, said there were several more requirements for a beer to be kosher.

The malt used in the beer must not be produced during the Jewish festival of Passover. The emulsifiers and filtering agents must not contain animal products and a rabbi must oversee the cleanliness of the production line.
Herrenhauser is aiming not only at millions of Jews across Europe, but at consumers looking for a "pure" product.

"Supervised means controlled, which I think is very, very important to the world today," Plancey, an adviser to Britain's Chief Rabbi, agreed. He referred to scares over mad cow disease, with Europe banning British beef products for fear of infection.

Manfred Middendorff, owner and managing director of the brewery, said the idea first came when a Russian importer asked if a kosher beer was available. He found no kosher beer was brewed in Europe or the United States, and saw the potential immediately.
"It's hard to find a marketing niche," he added.

The beer, priced at 90 pence ($1.50) a bottle in Britain, has already sold well on a test run in Germany, Spain, Norway and Hungary. "We sold 200 containers -- about five million pounds worth," Middendorff said.
If it sells well in Britain, Herrenhauser will look at the United States in mid-1997.
"If there had been 10 kosher beers in London I don't think it would have been worth it," said Peter Martin, U.K. sales manager for Premier World Wide Beers Plc, which markets Herrenhauser products.
"Coming into the U.K. with another good German beer is no news item."
And the Jewish community was not the only target. Vegetarians would be obvious buyers, as would young drinkers looking for a new status label.
"We do think it's not just for the Jewish community. It's a very trendy product," Middendorff told a news conference.
The beer itself did not differ from the brewery's other products, Middendorff said. "It's a typical German pilsner."
"Now I'm waiting for a kosher whiskey," said Rabbi Plancey, a Scot.
